oneonone.spec: 1:1 between Me (engineer) and my manager (remote, name Daniela). ~1400 words. Career growth, feedback on a recent incident postmortem, workload, she asks me to draft a proposal by Friday; vague maybe-plans.
oneonone.raw:
[00:00] Me: Hey Daniela, can you hear me okay? My mic was being weird earlier.
[00:04] Others: Yeah you're coming through fine. Sorry I'm a few minutes late, the last call ran over. Okay so, how's your week going
[00:12] Me: Pretty good, busy. I finally got the, uh, the rollout for the billing service out the door on Tuesday so that's a relief
[00:21] Others: Oh nice, yeah I saw that go out. Did it go smooth or was there the thing with the cache again
[00:28] Me: Mostly smooth. There was a little bit of the cache thing but it was like, way smaller, we caught it in staging this time which, you know, that's the whole point of the postmortem stuff
[00:39] Others: Right, yeah. I want to get into the postmortem actually, I read through it again last night and I have some thoughts. But first I wanted to check in on how you're doing generally. Like not just the tickets
[00:50] Me: Yeah, honestly, mixed. I've been feeling kind of like I'm treading water a little. Like I'm closing stuff but I don't feel like I'm, I don't know, growing into anything new
[01:03] Others: Mm. Okay, that's useful to hear. Say more about that
[01:07] Me: I guess, like, I've been on the same kind of work for like eight months. Integrations, bug fixes, the occasional migration. It's solid work but I want to be the person who designs the thing, not just the person who builds the thing someone else designed
[01:22] Others: Totally fair. And I think that's a reasonable read. Let's talk about what that could look like concretely. Is it the architecture side you're interested in, or more the, like, technical leadership on a project
[01:34] Me: Probably both? Like I'd love to own a design doc end to end. I did a little bit of that on the retry logic thing last spring and I really liked it, but it was like, a small piece
[01:46] Others: Yeah I remember that. Your design doc for the retry logic was actually really clean, Marcus pointed to it in the review. So I think you have the instincts, the question is just getting you more surface area
[01:58] Me: Thanks, that means a lot. Um, I think the thing is I don't know how to ask for it without it sounding like I'm trying to skip the grunt work
[02:08] Others: —no, I don't think that comes across that way at all. Honestly the grunt work is part of it. But I hear you, and I think we should just be explicit about it. Like, you can say I want to own X by Q3
[02:20] Me: Okay. Yeah. Q3 feels doable. Maybe the, uh, the event ingestion redesign? That's been sitting in the backlog forever and nobody really wants it
[02:31] Others: Ha, yeah, that's kind of the point, nobody wants it because it's gnarly. Let me think about that one. There's a version of it that conflicts with what Priya's team is doing on the pipeline side, and I don't want you walking into a turf thing without context. Can we park that and come back to it
[02:49] Me: Sure, yeah, park it. I didn't realize Priya's team was touching ingestion
[02:54] Others: They're not really, it's more the downstream consumers. I'll loop you in. Okay, postmortem. So I went through the timeline and I think the root cause section is good but I want the contributing factors to be sharper. Like, the alerting gap, that's listed as a bullet but it should probably be its own section
[03:14] Me: Yeah, I wasn't sure how much to lean into that because it kind of makes the on-call setup look bad, and the on-call setup is kind of Dev's thing
[03:24] Others: —I think you should lean into it. The point of a postmortem is not to make anyone look good or bad, it's to make the next incident less likely. If the alerting didn't fire for forty minutes, that's a fact and it's the most actionable thing in the doc
[03:38] Me: Okay. Yeah, that's fair. I'll pull it out. Should I also add the thing about the rollback runbook being out of date? I mentioned it in a comment but I didn't put it in the doc
[03:49] Others: Yes, definitely. That's a good catch. Put it in as an action item with an owner. Do you want to own that or should I assign it
[03:58] Me: I can take it. Maybe by end of next week? I'm not sure, I've got the proposal thing too
[04:05] Others: Oh right, the proposal. Yeah, so let's talk about that because I think it's the most important thing from this call. I'd like you to draft a proposal for the ingestion redesign. Not a full design doc, more like a one-pager with the problem, a couple of options, and a rough estimate. Can you get that to me by Friday
[04:24] Me: Friday. Um, yeah, I think so. Is Friday this Friday or the one after? Sorry, I'm trying to look at my calendar
[04:31] Others: This Friday. I know it's tight. If it slips to Monday that's fine, just let me know so I can plan around it
[04:39] Me: Okay, I'll aim for Friday. What should the, like, the audience be? Is it just you or is it going to Marcus and the leads
[04:48] Others: Start with me. I'll decide who else sees it after. But write it so Marcus could read it cold, because he'll probably ask about it
[04:58] Me: Got it. Yeah. Okay. The estimate part is kind of scary, I don't have great numbers on the current throughput. Like I know roughly but not exact
[05:08] Others: That's okay, rough is fine. Put in what you know and flag what you don't. And if you need the metrics, ask Joaquin, he's got the dashboards for the ingestion cluster, I think he set most of them up
[05:20] Me: Joaquin, okay. Yeah I'll ping him. Hopefully he's not swamped
[05:25] Others: He's always a little swamped. Tell him I said it's fine to give you twenty minutes
[05:31] Me: Ha, okay. Um, one other thing. I've been thinking about whether there's any path toward the staff track, or is that like a, a much longer thing
[05:42] Others: Yeah, I've been thinking about that too, honestly. I don't want to promise anything. The honest answer is it depends a lot on whether the ingestion work goes well and whether you can show that kind of cross-team scope. If the proposal lands and you lead it, that's a very real signal
[06:00] Me: Okay. Yeah. That's helpful. So it's kind of, like, prove it through the proposal
[06:06] Others: Sort of. I'd frame it as, this is an opportunity, not a test. But yes, I'd rather you know that the path runs through this kind of work than have you guess
[06:16] Me: Yeah, I appreciate that. Okay. I think I have a clearer picture now. Proposal by Friday, postmortem changes, rollback runbook, ping Joaquin
[06:26] Others: That's exactly it. And hey, I know the last few months have been heavy. Take the time you need on the runbook, it's not urgent in the way the proposal is
[06:36] Me: Thanks Daniela. Yeah, I'll try to take a breather this afternoon actually
[06:41] Others: Good. Okay, I have to jump, I've got another call at the top of the hour. Same time next week?
[06:47] Me: Yep, sounds good
[06:49] Others: Great. Talk soon
[06:50] Me: Bye

sales.spec: Sales/discovery call: Me is account exec at a dev-tools startup 'Lintly', Others = two people from prospect company 'Harbor Freight Logistics' (Marcus, ops lead; and a security person whose name is never said). ~2000 words. Pricing tiers, seat counts, SOC 2 question, pilot timeline, objections, next steps on both sides.
sales.raw:
[00:00] Me: Okay, I think we're live now, can you guys hear me okay? Great. Thanks for making the time, I know it's a crazy week for logistics stuff right now.
[00:09] Others: Yeah, yeah, no we can hear you. Marcus here, I'm ops lead at Harbor Freight, and I've got our security person on too, they're going to jump in when we get to the questions around data stuff.
[00:21] Me: Perfect, that's exactly who I wanted to have on. So just to kind of frame it, what I'd like to do in the next uh, like, thirty-five minutes or so is understand how your team's reviewing pull requests and CI stuff today, where it's breaking down, and then I'll walk through what Lintly does and we can see if it's a fit. Does that work for you?
[00:41] Others: Yeah that works. So basically right now we've got, um, like forty-something engineers spread across the platform team and the routing team and then a couple of contractors, and the honest answer is our code review is kind of a mess. Like reviews sit for days. Marcus—
[00:58] Others: —yeah sorry, the thing is we tried a couple of linters a few years back and everybody just turned them off because the noise was insane, like nine hundred warnings on day one.
[01:10] Me: Yeah, that's the number one thing we hear, honestly. So when you say reviews sit for days, do you have a sense of where in the process they're stalling? Is it waiting on a reviewer, or is it authors going back and forth fixing stuff that a tool should've caught before a human ever looked at it?
[01:28] Others: Oh it's definitely the second one. Like, it's a lot of, you know, style stuff, naming, unused imports, somebody forgot to handle an error return. Senior people are spending their review time on that instead of on the actual logic. And then on top of that our Jenkins setup is, um, it's held together with tape honestly. Half the pipeline times out.
[01:49] Me: Got it. And are you on Jenkins for everything or is some of it on GitHub Actions already?
[01:55] Others: Mostly Jenkins. There's a little bit of Actions for the mobile driver app team, they kind of went their own way. We're trying to figure out whether we consolidate or not, that's a whole other conversation.
[02:08] Me: Okay, that's helpful to know, because Lintly plugs into both, so you wouldn't have to make that call to get started. Let me actually show you what it looks like on a real PR, I'll share my screen. Can you see my screen?
[02:20] Others: Yeah, we see it. Is that a real repo?
[02:23] Me: It's a sample one but it's built from a fintech client's codebase, scrubbed. So what you're seeing here is a PR comment thread. The big difference is we only surface findings that the team has actually decided to enforce, and we rank them by severity, so the noise problem you described doesn't happen by default. Like on day one for most teams we start in what we call warn-only mode, which means nothing blocks a merge, it just annotates.
[02:52] Others: Okay, what happens to the nine hundred warnings then. Does it just dump all of them on us.
[02:58] Me: No, that's the thing. We do a baseline scan and we suppress existing findings, so you only see new issues introduced by the PR. The legacy stuff gets worked down over time on whatever schedule you want.
[03:11] Others: Huh. Okay. That's, yeah, that's the thing we actually need. Because I don't want to be the guy who makes everybody's life worse.
[03:19] Me: Totally fair. So let's talk numbers, because I know you're going to ask. Our pricing is per active developer seat per month. We've got three tiers. Team is, um, twenty-two dollars per seat per month billed annually, that gets you the core rules, Jenkins and Actions integrations, and standard support. Business is, uh, thirty-eight dollars, that adds custom rule authoring, SSO, and audit logs. And then Enterprise is custom, that's where you get the on-prem deployment and the dedicated success manager.
[03:52] Others: Okay. So with forty-five seats on Business that's, what, like, seventeen hundred a month?
[03:58] Me: Roughly seventeen-ten, yeah, so about twenty thousand four hundred a year. But I'd be careful with that number, because active seats is what matters, and we only count developers who opened or commented on a PR in the last thirty days. So if you've got contractors who've rolled off, you're not paying for them.
[04:17] Others: Our contractors are, uh, like, six of the forty-five, and two of them are leaving end of the month, so.
[04:23] Me: Right, so realistically you're probably looking at around thirty-nine active seats, depending on churn. I'd rather give you the accurate number now than have it be a surprise at renewal.
[04:34] Others: Appreciate that. Yeah.
[04:37] Others: —sorry, quick question from me, is the Business tier the one with the SSO? Because we're on Okta and that's kind of non-negotiable.
[04:46] Me: Yes, Business and up. We support SAML and SCIM with Okta, so provisioning and deprovisioning is automatic.
[04:54] Others: Okay, good. And the audit logs too?
[04:57] Me: Audit logs are in Business, yes. Exportable to your SIEM.

[05:03] Others: Okay so this is where I hand it over. Go ahead.
[05:07] Others: Hi, yeah, thanks. I'm the security lead here, I'll be quick. Before we go further I need to understand where our source code lives when Lintly processes it. Like, is it stored, for how long, is it used for training anything?
[05:22] Me: Good, that's the right question to ask first. So Lintly analyzes code in memory during the scan, and we retain only the findings metadata, not the source. We don't use customer code for training any model, that's in our terms and our DPA. Do you want me to pull up the data flow diagram?
[05:41] Others: Yeah please. And are you SOC 2?
[05:45] Me: So we're SOC 2 Type I, got that in March. We're in the observation window for Type II right now, which runs through, um, end of Q3, and we expect the report in October. I'd rather tell you that straight than let you find out later.
[06:01] Others: Okay. So Type I only, for now. That's a problem for us, honestly. Our procurement policy requires Type II for any vendor with source code access.
[06:12] Me: Yeah, I hear you, and I'd rather not oversell it. Can I ask, is the policy strict on Type II specifically, or is it something like a current SOC 2 report plus a bridge letter? Because I know some of our customers have gotten approved on that path while we finish the window.
[06:28] Others: I, uh, I don't know off the top of my head. I'd have to check with legal. Can you send over the Type I report and a pen test summary and I'll take it to them?
[06:38] Me: Absolutely, I'll send both today. And I'll also ask our compliance person if we can get a bridge letter from our auditor. I'll follow up by Thursday on that.
[06:48] Others: Okay. And the on-prem thing, is that available for Business or is that Enterprise? Because if we can keep the code inside our VPC that'd probably clear a lot of this.
[06:59] Me: On-prem is Enterprise only, and honestly it's a heavier lift, usually a few weeks of setup with our solutions team. But it's worth raising. If the data residency is the blocker, we can at least scope it.
[07:12] Others: Yeah, it's probably the blocker. Like if legal says no to SaaS-only we're stuck.
[07:18] Me: Got it. Let's keep that on the table and figure it out in parallel with the Type I docs, so we don't lose time.
[07:25] Others: —yeah, no, that works. Marcus, you still there?
[07:29] Others: Yeah, I'm here. Look, from the ops side the pilot is what I care about. Can we do a pilot with, like, the platform team only? Maybe eight to ten people, six weeks?
[07:40] Me: Yeah, a pilot with the platform team is a really clean way to start. Typically we'd set success criteria up front, things like time-to-merge on PRs, number of review comments that are style-related, and developer sentiment at the end. Would you want to define those together?
[07:58] Others: Yes. Like we'd want to see review cycle time drop, that's the number the VP cares about. Right now median is, uh, like three days to first review and then another day or two of back and forth.
[08:12] Me: Okay, that's a clear metric. We can baseline it from your Jenkins and GitHub data during the first week so we're not guessing later. And if we do the pilot on the platform team, would it be warn-only the whole time, or do you want to flip on blocking for some rules?
[08:28] Others: Warn-only for the first two weeks at least. Then maybe we block on a small set, like the security stuff and nothing else. Is that possible?
[08:37] Me: Absolutely, you'd pick the rule set per severity, so blocking on security-category findings only is totally doable.
[08:44] Others: Okay. Timeline. When could we realistically start?
[08:49] Me: If we get the paperwork moving this week, we could have the pilot environment set up by, let's say, the twenty-eighth. That would put the six-week window ending around the middle of next month. Does that line up with your sprint planning?
[09:05] Others: Hmm, we've got a release freeze the first week of the month, so maybe the start date slips to the seventh. Let me check with the platform lead.
[09:15] Me: Okay, I'll put a hold on the seventh tentatively and we'll confirm. What's the freeze actually cover? Is it just prod deploys or the whole dev workflow?
[09:25] Others: Just prod deploys I think. Dev workflow keeps running. But honestly our engineers will be buried in the freeze anyway so adoption might be slow that week.
[09:35] Me: That's fair. Then maybe we don't count the first week against the adoption metrics, we just treat it as setup. Sound reasonable?
[09:44] Others: Yeah, that's reasonable.
[09:47] Others: —also sorry, one more thing from the security side. Do you guys have anything for secrets detection? Because that's the one that scares me most. Somebody commits an AWS key and it's in history forever.
[10:00] Me: We do have secret scanning as part of the security rule pack, it catches common credential patterns and high-entropy strings. It's not a full replacement for something like a dedicated secrets vault or GitHub's push protection, but it works alongside those. Is that the kind of coverage you're after?
[10:18] Others: Yeah. And it'd block the commit, or just flag it?
[10:22] Me: It can block the PR merge. It doesn't block the commit locally unless you install our pre-commit hook, which is optional.
[10:31] Others: Okay, I'd want the pre-commit hook on. Can you put that in the pilot scope?
[10:36] Me: Yep, I'll add it to the pilot setup doc.
[10:40] Others: Thanks. Okay, I think that covers most of what I needed.
[10:46] Me: Great. Let me recap so we're on the same page. On my side I'm sending the Type I report and the pen test summary today, I'm checking with our auditor about a bridge letter and I'll follow up by Thursday, I'm also confirming whether on-prem scoping is worth doing for Enterprise, and I'm putting a tentative hold on the seventh for pilot kickoff with the pre-commit hook in scope. Does that sound right?
[11:09] Others: That's right. On our side I'm getting the platform lead to confirm the seventh and the pilot group, and I'll get the security person's questions to legal about the Type II policy, and I'll ask whether a bridge letter is acceptable. Oh and we need a rough cost approval for the pilot, can you send us a quote for the thirty-nine seats on Business?
[11:31] Me: Yes, I'll send a quote for thirty-nine seats on Business, and I'll note the pilot is discounted or free, what do you need on that?
[11:40] Others: Let's say we'd pay for it but we want a pilot rate, maybe the first six weeks at half price, so it's easier to get signed off as a line item.
[11:50] Me: I can get approval on a pilot rate. I'll run that by my manager and come back with a number before Thursday too.
[11:57] Others: Perfect. Okay, I think we're good. Thanks for the time, this was actually more useful than the last three vendor calls.
[12:05] Me: Really glad to hear it. Thanks Marcus, and thanks to your security lead as well, those questions were sharp. I'll send the follow-up email in the next hour.
[12:14] Others: Sounds good. Talk soon.

planning.spec: Product planning for Q1 at a note-taking app. Me = PM, Others = designer (Sven) and eng lead (Aiko) - merged as Others. ~2500 words. Prioritizing 5 features, some decided, some deferred, one disagreement left unresolved.
planning.raw:
[00:00] Me: Okay, can everybody hear me? Yeah? Cool. So um, this is the Q1 planning sync, we've got about forty minutes. Last time we had like nine candidate features on the board and I want to get down to five today and actually make calls on a few of them, so that's the goal.
[00:19] Others: yeah sounds good, I can hear you fine. I've got the board open, I moved the offline sync card to the top because I think it's the one everybody's been asking about.
[00:28] Me: Right, offline sync. Okay. Before we get into that, can we just quickly do the ones we already agreed on in the last two weeks so we don't re-litigate them. So the the template gallery is in, yeah? Aiko you said the backend is done?
[00:44] Others: Yeah the template gallery backend is merged, it's behind a flag right now. Um, we still need the thumbnails to load lazily, that's like a half-day thing, but functionally it's there. I'd say it's ready for internal dogfooding this week.
[00:58] Others: Also I want to say, Sven's mockups for the gallery are the cleanest thing we've done in a while, like I actually didn't have to ask follow up questions.
[01:06] Me: Ha, okay, that's good to hear. Sven you there?
[01:09] Others: Yeah I'm here, thanks. Yeah the gallery was a good one, it's mostly just reusing the card component from search. Um, I did flag one thing, the empty state for when someone has zero templates saved, I haven't really figured that out yet, I'll have something by Thursday.
[01:24] Me: Okay, put that on the tracker. So template gallery: in, internal this week, external beta target is like the end of January. Yeah? Everybody good with that date?
[01:35] Others: I think end of January is tight but doable if the lazy loading is done by the twentieth.
[01:41] Me: Okay, we'll say twentieth for lazy loading as a checkpoint. Next thing, the the import from Notion and Evernote, that's the one we pushed to Q2 right? Because of the parser stuff.
[01:53] Others: Yeah, Q2. Like we said, the Evernote export format is a mess, the nested tables alone are a nightmare, and I don't want to ship a half-working importer and have people lose formatting. So I'd rather we just own that as a Q2 thing and be honest about it.
[02:10] Me: Yeah agreed. I'll write it in the roadmap doc as deferred with the reason, the nested tables thing, so we don't get asked about it every single week. Okay. So um, next is the one I actually wanted to spend time on, which is offline sync.
[02:26] Others: Yeah. So from the eng side, I want to be clear about what offline sync actually means here, because I feel like everybody in the room has a slightly different picture. Like do we mean you can read your notes offline, or can you edit offline and have it reconcile when you come back online, or do we mean full conflict resolution across devices?
[02:46] Me: Good question. I think the user ask, the one that keeps coming up in support tickets, is the edit offline and sync when reconnected. Like people on planes, people in the subway. Reading offline we kind of already half have from the cache, right?
[03:02] Others: Half, yeah. The cache holds the last synced state, but it's not guaranteed, like if you open a note you haven't looked at in a month it might not be there. So reading is a reliability thing more than a feature thing. Editing with reconciliation is the real project. And honestly the reconciliation is where all the hard parts are.
[03:22] Me: How big is the hard part? Give me a number, even a rough one, I'm going to get asked.
[03:28] Others: Um. If we do it properly with CRDTs, like the text-level merge, I'd say six to eight engineer weeks just for the core, and then the mobile clients are a separate chunk, maybe another three or four weeks. So realistically it's a quarter for two engineers if nothing goes sideways. And something always goes sideways.
[03:50] Me: Okay. Okay, that's a big chunk for Q1. Sven, from the design side, what does offline look like to the user? Because I feel like there's a lot of UI surface there.
[04:02] Others: Yeah, so, I think the biggest design question is how do we tell the user the state of their note. Like when you're offline and you edit something, you need to know it's saved locally and it's going to sync, and when there's a conflict you need to know that too, and you need to be able to resolve it without it being scary. I've sketched three options. Um, one is just a little cloud icon in the corner, very quiet. Two is a banner that appears when you're offline. Three is a per-note indicator, which I think is the most honest but also the most visual noise.
[04:36] Others: The conflict UX is the part I'm least sure about. I don't want a modal that says "conflict detected," that's terrible, people just click whatever. I think we need to show both versions side by side and let them pick or merge, and that's a whole screen I haven't designed yet.
[04:54] Me: So that's more design time too. Okay. Sven how many weeks for the conflict screen?

design_review.spec: 25-minute technical design review of migrating a job queue from Redis to Postgres (using SKIP LOCKED) at a fintech. Me presents; Others = 3 senior engineers (Fatima, Greg, Ola). ~3400 words, lots of jargon (pgbouncer, idempotency keys, p99 latency, Kafka), ASR mangles jargon. Decisions, risks, 2 open questions, multiple owners with dates.
design_review.raw:
[00:00] Me: Okay can everyone hear me alright? Cool. So this is the design review for moving the payouts job queue off Redis and onto Postgres, using SKIP LOCKED. I wanted to get it in front of you before we commit to anything. Um, I put the doc in the channel, it's about eleven pages, but the short version is we're replacing the Redis-backed queue that handles settlement retries and webhook fanout.
[00:19] Others: Yeah I read it. Fatima here, quick question before we dive in, when you say the queue handles settlement retries, does that include the ones that go out to the card processor or just internal stuff?
[00:31] Me: Both, so the card processor retries are the bulk of it. Like ninety-something percent of volume. Internal fanout is small but it's latency sensitive.
[00:40] Others: Right. Okay. Go ahead, sorry.
[00:43] Me: No, that's fine. So the motivation is basically three things. One, we've had two incidents in the last quarter where Redis evicted keys under memory pressure and we silently dropped jobs. Two, we don't have transactional enqueue, so the job gets written to Redis after the Postgres commit and if the process dies between those two we get a ghost payout state. Three, operationally we already run Postgres with, uh, pgbouncer in front of it, so we're not adding a new stateful system. That last one is kind of the big one for me.
[01:14] Others: Greg. Can I push on the eviction thing? Like did you confirm it was eviction and not a maxmemory-policy misconfig? Because I've seen teams blame eviction when the real issue was the noeviction policy returning OOM errors that the client swallowed.
[01:31] Me: Oh. Um. I, yeah, I checked the postmortem and it says eviction, the INFO stats showed evicted_keys going up, so I think it's real eviction. But I'd have to double check the client side.
[01:44] Others: Okay because that matters, cause if the client was swallowing errors then the fix is in the client and not the broker. Can you run that down?
[01:52] Me: Yeah, I'll take that. I'll pull the client error logs for both incident windows and post in the doc. Say by Thursday the twenty-third.
[02:01] Others: Thursday's fine. Ola you had something?
[02:04] Others: Yeah, so, um, my bigger concern is the idempotency story. Right now the Redis queue, the consumer acks, and the payout service uses an idempotency key that's the job ID. If we move to Postgres with SKIP LOCKED, the lock is held inside a transaction, and if the card processor call succeeds but the commit fails, we're going to re-run the job. Does the design have the idempotency key stored in the same transaction as the state change, or does it call the processor outside the transaction?
[02:37] Me: So, it's outside the transaction. Um, we take the lock, we mark the row in_progress, we commit, then we call the processor with the job ID as the idempotency key, then we open a second transaction to mark complete. So the processor is the source of truth for whether it succeeded and we rely on their idempotency to dedupe.
[02:58] Others: Okay so that's basically the same as the Redis flow, the processor dedupes. Is that actually guaranteed by the processor for how long? Because I thought their idempotency window was twenty-four hours and our retries can go out to like three days.
[03:13] Me: Yeah, that's, that's one of the open questions. I haven't gotten a confirmed answer from their account team on the window. The doc says twenty-four hours from the sales deck but I don't trust that.
[03:24] Others: Right, so that's a real gap. If a retry lands after the window, we double charge. That's not a latency issue, that's a money issue.
[03:33] Me: Agreed. So I think we need either a local idempotency table keyed on job ID with the processor response stored, or we cap retries inside the window. I put both in the doc but I lean toward the local table.
[03:47] Others: Local table. Definitely. Storing the response means we can also replay the outcome without calling them again.
[03:54] Others: Yeah, and that, uh, that adds a write per payout though. What's the throughput we're assuming? Because if we're at like, what, four hundred payouts a second at peak, that's a lot of extra rows.
[04:08] Me: So peak is about three hundred and forty a second, measured over the last month. Um, the local table would be one insert plus one update per job, so roughly seven hundred writes a second at peak on top of the queue traffic. I think Postgres can handle that on the primary but I haven't load tested it.
[04:27] Others: Okay, that's the kind of thing I'd want a number on before we commit. What's p99 on the current Redis enqueue to dequeue path? Do we have that?
[04:36] Me: Um, p99 end to end is around forty milliseconds. Enqueue is sub-millisecond. Dequeue with the blocking pop is basically instant when there's work.
[04:46] Others: And what do you expect on SKIP LOCKED? Because polling is going to add latency unless you're using LISTEN/NOTIFY, and LISTEN/NOTIFY through pgbouncer in transaction mode is, um, it's a mess, you can't hold the LISTEN connection.
[05:02] Me: Yeah, so the doc proposes polling with a backoff, starting at fifty milliseconds and capping at five hundred when the queue is empty. Under load it should be near-immediate because workers will always find rows. I expect p99 to be maybe a hundred and twenty milliseconds, but I'm not confident in that.
[05:21] Others: A hundred and twenty is a lot higher than forty. Is that acceptable for the webhook fanout path? I think that one is the latency sensitive one you said earlier.
[05:31] Me: Right. So for webhook fanout I'd propose we keep Redis for now. Or, uh, we could split it. Fanout stays on Redis, settlement moves to Postgres. That's a smaller blast radius too.
[05:44] Others: Two systems is worse operationally though. You're keeping Redis around forever.
[05:50] Others: Hmm, I don't know that it's forever. Like we could do the fanout on Kafka later, which we're already partway through the migration on for the ledger events. Um, I'd rather not add more Kafka topics right now though, the consumer lag alerts have been noisy.
[06:08] Others: Yeah the lag alerts are a whole thing. Okay so I'm hearing: settlement to Postgres, fanout stays on Redis short term, and we revisit fanout after the Kafka consumer group stuff settles.
[06:20] Me: Yes, that's what I'd write down. Can someone own the fanout revisit? I don't want it to become Redis forever.
[06:27] Others: I'll take that. Greg, you're on the ledger Kafka work anyway, right?
[06:33] Others: Yeah I can own the decision doc for fanout. Say by the end of next sprint, so March the fourteenth.
[06:40] Me: Perfect. Um, and on the pgbouncer side, I'd like Ola or someone to review the pool config. We're proposing transaction pooling with SKIP LOCKED, which should be fine because each claim is a short transaction, but long-running holds would be bad.
[06:56] Others: Yeah I'll review it. The thing to check is whether any worker holds a session-level thing like advisory locks or prepared statements, because transaction mode breaks those. Do we use prepared statements in the queue client?
[07:12] Me: I, I think the Go driver uses them by default? Um. I'd have to check. I think we set the simple protocol but I'm not sure that's in the doc.
[07:22] Others: Okay, that's a must-check. If the driver is caching prepared statements under transaction pooling you'll get weird errors that look random. I've seen it take down a whole service.
[07:33] Others: Fatima, sorry, you had a risk list?
[07:37] Others: Yeah, a few things. First, rollback. How do we get back to Redis if Postgres falls over at two in the morning? The doc says feature flag per queue, but the in-flight jobs are the problem. If half the jobs are in Postgres and we flip back, who drains them?
[07:55] Me: So, um, the plan is dual-write for one week where we enqueue to both but only consume from one, and the rollback is flipping the consumer. The dual-write doubles the enqueue cost but it's cheap.
[08:08] Others: Dual write is its own bug source though. If the two writes diverge we get jobs that run twice or never. How are we reconciling?
[08:17] Me: Um, we have a nightly reconciliation job that compares the two sides by job ID. Owned by, I think, Priya's team? I'd need to confirm.
[08:26] Others: Priya's team owns the reconciler, yeah. But it's currently built for the ledger, not the queue. That's a gap to note.
[08:34] Others: Okay, let me try to summarize where we are. Decisions: settlement moves to Postgres with SKIP LOCKED, polling with backoff, fanout stays on Redis for now, and we go with a local idempotency table rather than relying on the processor window. Risks: the eviction root cause may be client-side, the processor idempotency window is unverified, the pool mode might break prepared statements, and dual-write reconciliation isn't built for queues.
[09:02] Me: Yep. And the two open questions are, one, what's the real processor idempotency window, and two, does the Go driver use prepared statements under our pool config.
[09:12] Others: Right. Those two gate the design. Can someone own the processor question?
[09:17] Others: I can ping the processor account team. Ola, can you own the driver check?
[09:23] Others: Yeah. Today's the eleventh, so I'll have it by the eighteenth.
[09:28] Me: Great. And I'll own the load test on the idempotency table, target is the end of the month, March the twenty-eighth, and the client error log pull by the twenty-third like I said.
[09:40] Others: Sounds good. Any objections to proceeding to a prototype once those are answered?
[09:46] Others: No objection from me, but I want the load test numbers before we greenlight prod.
[09:52] Others: Agreed.
[09:54] Me: Okay, I'll write all this up in the doc and tag owners. Thanks everyone, that was really useful.
[10:01] Others: Thanks.

customer_support.spec: Escalation call: Me (support engineer) with an upset customer (Others) about data sync failures in a mobile app. ~1100 words. Repro steps, versions (iOS 18.2, app 4.11.3), workaround offered, customer demands refund credit, Me promises to check with billing, not committed.
customer_support.raw:
[00:00] Me: Hi, thanks for hopping on. This is Dana, I'm on the support engineering side, so I'm, um, I'm going to try to get to the bottom of the sync issue with you today.
[00:12] Others: Yeah, okay. Honestly I've been told that three times now and nothing has changed, so I'm just going to say it up front. Our field team has been unable to get data to sync for almost two weeks and it's costing us real money.
[00:27] Me: I hear you, and I'm sorry it's been that long. Can you tell me, um, who's on the call with you on your side?
[00:35] Others: It's me, Marcus, I run ops for the northeast region. Dev Patel is on from our IT side, he's the one who's been reinstalling stuff. Maybe, I don't know, maybe he's muted.
[00:46] Me: Got it, Marcus, Dev, thanks. So what I have in the notes is that you're on app version four point eleven point three, and the devices are running iOS eighteen point two. Is that right?
[00:58] Others: Yeah, that's, that's what the admin console says. Like I said, we've reinstalled. Twice. Dev wiped one of the phones completely.
[01:08] Me: Okay. So when a tech goes offline, say in a basement site or a rural job, what happens when they come back into signal? Walk me through what they see.
[01:19] Others: They, so the job shows as completed on the phone. The photos are there, the checklist is there, the signature. But then on the dashboard in the office, it's just not there. Or it's there but it's half, like the checklist shows up and the photos don't.
[01:38] Dev Patel: Yeah, and sometimes it's the opposite, the photos come through and the job record is stuck at, uh, pending sync forever.
[01:46] Me: Okay, that's really helpful, Dev. Do you know roughly how many of the jobs are affected? Like is it every offline job or a subset?
[01:55] Others: It's, I'd say maybe one in four? Could be more. We pulled a report Thursday and it was like, I want to say forty-one jobs out of a hundred and sixty for that week were incomplete on the server side.
[02:10] Dev Patel: It was a hundred and sixty-three, I checked. Forty-one is the right number though.
[02:15] Me: Okay, forty-one of a hundred sixty-three. Thank you. Has this been consistent since, um, since when? Do you remember the first time you saw it?
[02:25] Others: The update. Or, no. We had the update go out like the eighth, and I think the first complaints came like the tenth. So right after. And it's gotten worse, not better, I'll be honest.
[02:40] Me: The eighth, that lines up with when the four point eleven point three build rolled out to your org. I want to be careful not to speculate too much before we reproduce it, but that's a useful timeline. Can I ask you to try something with me while we're on the call? Would Dev be able to do a repro?
[02:58] Dev Patel: Yeah, I can do it, I've got a test device on my desk. I'm, uh, I'm sharing my screen, can you see it?
[03:06] Me: I can't see a share yet, I'm, one sec. Okay, there it is, I see the app. Okay. So what we want is airplane mode on, create a job, fill out the checklist, take two photos, get a signature, then go to a different screen, then turn airplane mode off. Can you do that?
[03:26] Dev Patel: Yeah, yeah. Airplane on. Okay, new job, call it test one. Checklist, filling it, uh, all the boxes. Photo, photo. Signature. Save. Okay, airplane off.
[03:42] Me: Great. Now, just watch the sync indicator in the corner. Does it spin?
[03:48] Dev Patel: It spun for, like, a second. And now it says synced. So that's, I mean, it looks fine on the device.
[03:55] Me: Okay. Now the important part, can you go to the web dashboard? I'm going to ask Marcus to pull it up on his side too, Marcus, if you can refresh the job list and search for test one.
[04:07] Others: Hang on. Okay. Refreshing. Nope, I don't see test one. Let me, okay, I see a job from this morning but it's, it's got no photos attached. The checklist's there.
[04:22] Me: Okay, so that matches what you described. Dev, can you confirm on the device that the photos are actually attached to the job and not just sitting in the camera roll?
[04:33] Dev Patel: They're in the job. I can open them. It's, yeah, they're on the device.
[04:40] Me: Right. So the device side is recording the data correctly, and the server side is either not receiving the attachments or dropping them. That's a useful split for our engineers. I don't want to claim root cause yet, but this is a reproducible case, which is the first thing we needed.
[05:00] Others: Okay, but I need you to hear this. Reproducing it doesn't fix anything for my guys. I've got technicians sitting in trucks right now who can't close out jobs. We are three weeks from a contract renewal and this is exactly the kind of thing that makes me look bad to my own VP.
[05:19] Me: Understood. I completely understand the pressure, Marcus. And I want to be upfront that, um, I can't promise you a fix date on this call, because I don't own the engineering timeline. What I can do is escalate it with the reproduction steps we just walked through, flag it as affecting your region and the version rollout, and get it in front of the sync team today.
[05:42] Dev Patel: Can we get a workaround in the meantime though? Because my guys really can't wait.
[05:48] Me: Yes, there's a workaround that should help. Um, the thing that's worked for some other customers on this build is to keep the app in the foreground for about thirty seconds after reconnecting, and then force a manual sync from the job menu, rather than waiting for the automatic one. It's not perfect, but it reduced failures for a couple of teams. Dev, can you try that on test two?
[06:12] Dev Patel: Okay. Airplane on, new job, test two, same stuff. Airplane off, I'm, okay I'm holding it, thirty seconds, now manual sync. Okay, it says synced. Let me check the, yeah, refreshing on the web, okay, test two is there. Photos are there. Huh.
[06:32] Me: Okay, that's encouraging. One success isn't proof, so I'd want you to try a few more over the next day before you rely on it. And, Marcus, if you want, I can send a short written version of that workaround to your team.
[06:46] Others: Fine. Send it. But that's a band-aid. Your team is asking my technicians to babysit their phones. That's not a product. It's a, it's, honestly it's embarrassing that we're paying for this.
[07:00] Me: I hear you, and I'm not going to argue that it's ideal. You're right that it's a workaround and not a fix.
[07:08] Others: And I'm going to need something on the money side. We've lost, I calculated it, roughly nine to eleven thousand dollars in labor on re-dispatches over the last two weeks. Some of my guys have been driving back out to sites to redo work that was already done. I want a credit for that. Not a discount on next year. A credit on this invoice.
[07:31] Me: Okay. I can see why that's a serious cost, and I'm glad you put a number on it. I'm not able to approve a credit or refund myself, that's a decision for our billing team, so I can't commit to an amount or a yes on this call.
[07:47] Others: Then who can? Because I'm not going to keep paying full price for an app that doesn't do its one job.
[07:54] Me: I understand. What I can do is take the re-dispatch figures you just gave me, plus the report with the forty-one of a hundred sixty-three, and send them to billing today with a note that this is an escalation. I'll ask them to get back to you directly. I can't promise the outcome, but I can promise they'll see it with the context.
[08:14] Others: Today. You'll send it today.
[08:17] Me: I'll send it today, yes. And I'll copy you on the email so you have a record.
[08:23] Dev Patel: Can you also put the repro steps in there? Test one, the airplane thing. I want billing to see it's not us doing something weird.
[08:31] Me: Yes, I'll include the repro steps and the version numbers, four point eleven point three on iOS eighteen point two, so it's documented.
[08:40] Others: Okay. Look, I'm not trying to be a jerk here. I just need someone on your side to take this seriously.
[08:47] Me: I do take it seriously, Marcus. I know this isn't the call you wanted, and I'm sorry it's taken this long to get to someone who can actually see it through. Let me recap so we're aligned: I'm escalating the sync failure with the repro today, you have a workaround to try, I'm sending the billing request with your re-dispatch figures today, and I'll copy you. I'm not committing on the credit itself.
[09:10] Others: Yeah. Okay. That's, that's what I got. Send me the written stuff.
[09:16] Me: Will do. And, um, if the workaround stops working or you get new failures, reply directly to that thread and flag it as a regression so it doesn't sit in the queue.
[09:27] Dev Patel: Got it. Thanks, I think.
[09:30] Others: Yeah. Alright. Talk soon, I guess.
[09:34] Me: Thanks, Marcus, thanks Dev. Talk soon.
